text: In Jackson's knowledge argument, Mary learns all physical facts about colour in a black-and-white room, then sees red. The 'ability hypothesis' (Lewis, Nemirow) replies that Mary:
choices: learns a new non-physical fact, so physicalism is false.
gains no new propositional knowledge but new abilities to recognize, imagine, and remember red, so no non-physical fact is learned.
already knew what red looks like, so on seeing it she learns nothing whatever.
acquires a new phenomenal concept that refers to an old physical fact under a new mode of presentation.
explanation: The ability hypothesis concedes Mary gains something but reconstrues it as know-how (recognizing, imagining, remembering) rather than knowledge of a new fact, blocking the anti-physicalist conclusion. 'Learns a new non-physical fact' is Jackson's own dualist reading (the argument's conclusion), while the 'new phenomenal concept' reply is the distinct phenomenal concept strategy of Loar and Papineau.
